questions.stem: A company has 200 switches, each with its own local admin accounts. Whenever an administrator leaves, someone has to log in to every switch to remove that account. What is the underlying limitation?

options.text: Local authentication stores credentials on each device, so it doesn't scale; central AAA such as RADIUS or TACACS+ solves this
options.rationale: Correct: one central account store replaces 200 separate ones.

options.text: The accounts were created with 'secret' instead of 'password'
options.rationale: 'secret' is the better choice, and it has nothing to do with scaling.

options.text: 'login local' disables SSH
options.rationale: 'login local' works with SSH and Telnet alike.

options.text: Local accounts can't be given privilege level 15
options.rationale: They can; 'privilege 15' is set on local accounts all the time.

questions.explanation: With local authentication, credentials live on each device, so every change must be repeated everywhere. That doesn't scale, which is why larger networks move to central AAA.
questions.discriminator_tested: Local authentication doesn't scale; credentials live on each device.

questions.stem: Which two pairings of an iAAA step with the question it answers are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: Authentication: 'Prove it.'
options.rationale: Correct: it verifies the claimed identity.

options.text: Accounting: 'What did you do?'
options.rationale: Correct: it records activity.

options.text: Authorization: 'Who are you?'
options.rationale: 'Who are you?' is identification.

options.text: Identification: 'What may you do?'
options.rationale: 'What may you do?' is authorization.

options.text: Authentication: 'What did you do?'
options.rationale: 'What did you do?' is accounting.

questions.explanation: The iAAA model: identification asks who are you, authentication says prove it, authorization asks what may you do, and accounting asks what did you do.
questions.discriminator_tested: Who are you? Prove it. What may you do? What did you do?

questions.stem: Which two are 'something you have' authentication factors? (Choose two.)

options.text: A hardware security token
options.rationale: Correct: a physical object the user possesses.

options.text: A smart card
options.rationale: Correct: a physical object the user possesses.

options.text: A PIN
options.rationale: A PIN is something you know.

options.text: A fingerprint
options.rationale: A fingerprint is something you are.

options.text: A password
options.rationale: A password is something you know.

questions.explanation: Authentication verifies a claimed identity using factors from three categories: something you know (password, PIN), something you have (token, smart card), and something you are (biometrics).
questions.discriminator_tested: Factor categories: know, have, are.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT MFA?

options.text: A password plus the answer to a security question
options.rationale: Correct choice: both are something you know, so it is one category.

options.text: A password plus a code from an authenticator app
options.rationale: MFA: something you know plus something you have.

options.text: A smart card plus a PIN
options.rationale: MFA: something you have plus something you know.

options.text: A fingerprint plus a password
options.rationale: MFA: something you are plus something you know.

questions.explanation: MFA requires two or more different factor categories. Two items of the same kind, such as a password and a security answer, are still a single factor category.
questions.discriminator_tested: MFA factors must come from different categories.

questions.stem: Which statement about MFA methods is NOT true?

options.text: SMS codes can't be intercepted, because they travel over the phone network
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: SMS codes can be intercepted or redirected, for example through SIM swapping.

options.text: Time-based hardware or software tokens are generally stronger
options.rationale: True: codes are generated locally.

options.text: An emailed code is only as safe as the email account
options.rationale: True.

options.text: Codes delivered by voice call can be redirected
options.rationale: True: through call forwarding or a hijacked number.

questions.explanation: MFA methods include email, SMS, voice call, and time-based tokens. Time-based tokens are generally stronger; codes sent by SMS, voice, or email can be intercepted or redirected.
questions.discriminator_tested: SMS, voice, and email codes can be intercepted; time-based tokens are stronger.

questions.stem: When does authorization happen relative to authentication, and what does it decide?

options.text: After authentication; it decides what the authenticated user may access or do
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Before authentication; it decides who the user is
options.rationale: Identity is established first, by identification and authentication.

options.text: At the same time as accounting; it records what the user did
options.rationale: Recording activity is accounting.

options.text: Only when the user logs out
options.rationale: Authorization decisions are made while the user is working.

questions.explanation: Authorization determines what an authenticated user may access or do, so it can only happen after authentication has proven who they are.
questions.discriminator_tested: Authorization happens after authentication.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT part of identity and access management (IAM)?

options.text: Choosing nonoverlapping Wi-Fi channels for the access points
options.rationale: Correct choice: that is wireless network design, not identity management.

options.text: Creating accounts when people join the organization
options.rationale: Part of IAM: the start of the identity lifecycle.

options.text: Changing access when people move to a new role
options.rationale: Part of IAM.

options.text: Removing access when people leave
options.rationale: Part of IAM: the end of the lifecycle.

questions.explanation: Identity and access management covers the processes and tools that manage identities and their access across their lifecycle: joining, changing roles, and leaving. AAA is one mechanism inside it.
questions.discriminator_tested: IAM manages identities and access across their lifecycle.

questions.stem: An organization applies least privilege to every account. Which harm does this most directly reduce?

options.text: The damage that a compromised account, a mistake, or a malicious insider can cause
options.rationale: Correct: each account can only do what its job needs.

options.text: Wi-Fi interference from microwave ovens
options.rationale: That is a radio problem, not an access problem.

options.text: Phishing emails reaching users' inboxes
options.rationale: Least privilege limits what happens after a compromise; it doesn't filter email.

options.text: Port scans from the internet
options.rationale: Scans are handled by firewalls and IDS/IPS.

questions.explanation: Least privilege grants only the access needed for the job. It limits the damage from mistakes, malware, and insiders, because no account holds more power than it needs.
questions.discriminator_tested: Least privilege limits damage from mistakes, malware, and insiders.

questions.stem: Which statement about RBAC is NOT true?

options.text: Each permission is assigned directly to individual users, one by one
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: in RBAC, permissions attach to roles.

options.text: Permissions attach to roles
options.rationale: True: this defines RBAC.

options.text: Users get access through the roles they hold
options.rationale: True.

options.text: When someone changes jobs, their role membership is what changes
options.rationale: True: that is what makes RBAC easy to manage.

questions.explanation: In role-based access control (RBAC), permissions attach to roles, and users get access through their role rather than through individual assignment.
questions.discriminator_tested: RBAC is role-based, not per-individual.

questions.stem: Which two are examples of accounting? (Choose two.)

options.text: A log of every command an administrator ran on a router, with timestamps
options.rationale: Correct: a record of what was done and when.

options.text: Records of each user's login and logout times and session data
options.rationale: Correct: an audit trail of sessions.

options.text: Checking a user's password at login
options.rationale: That is authentication.

options.text: Deciding that a user may read a file but not change it
options.rationale: That is authorization.

options.text: Asking the user for a username
options.rationale: That is identification.

questions.explanation: Accounting records who did what and when, such as logins, commands, and session data. It is the after-the-fact audit trail, distinct from proving identity or granting access.
questions.discriminator_tested: Accounting is the after-the-fact audit trail.

questions.stem: Which statement about RADIUS is NOT true?

options.text: It encrypts the entire packet payload
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: RADIUS encrypts only the password in the request.

options.text: It uses UDP 1812 for authentication and 1813 for accounting
options.rationale: True.

options.text: It is an open standard
options.rationale: True.

options.text: It is typical for network access such as 802.1X, Wi-Fi, and VPN
options.rationale: True.

questions.explanation: RADIUS is open-standard, centralized AAA over UDP 1812/1813. It combines authentication and authorization, encrypts only the password, and is typical for network access.
questions.discriminator_tested: RADIUS encrypts only the password; TACACS+ encrypts the whole payload.

questions.stem: Which two statements correctly distinguish TACACS+ from RADIUS? (Choose two.)

options.text: TACACS+ uses TCP 49; RADIUS uses UDP
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: TACACS+ encrypts the entire payload; RADIUS encrypts only the password
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: TACACS+ combines authentication and authorization; RADIUS separates them
options.rationale: This is reversed: TACACS+ separates them and RADIUS combines them.

options.text: RADIUS was originated by Cisco
options.rationale: TACACS+ is the Cisco-originated protocol; RADIUS is an open standard.

options.text: TACACS+ is mainly used for user Wi-Fi access
options.rationale: RADIUS is typical for network access; TACACS+ is typical for device administration.

questions.explanation: TACACS+ runs over TCP 49, encrypts the entire payload, and separates authentication, authorization, and accounting, which suits device administration. RADIUS uses UDP, encrypts only the password, and suits network access.
questions.discriminator_tested: TACACS+: TCP 49, full encryption, separate A/A/A; RADIUS: UDP, password only.

questions.stem: Which order of steps is correct when configuring iAAA on a Cisco device?

options.text: Enable AAA, define the AAA server, build the method lists, then apply the lists to the lines
options.rationale: Correct: AAA must be on, and a list must exist before it can be applied.

options.text: Apply the method lists to the lines, enable AAA, then build the lists
options.rationale: You can't apply lists that don't exist yet.

options.text: Define the server, apply the lists to the lines, enable AAA, then build the lists
options.rationale: AAA comes on last here, and lists are applied before they are built.

options.text: Build the lists, apply them, define the server, and never enable AAA
options.rationale: Nothing takes effect until AAA is enabled.

questions.explanation: Configuring iAAA means enabling AAA, defining the server, building method lists for authentication, authorization, and accounting, and applying them to lines. The order within each method list also matters.
questions.discriminator_tested: Enable AAA, define the server, build method lists, apply to lines.

questions.stem: Which statement about the RADIUS login process is NOT true?

options.text: The user's laptop is the RADIUS client and sends the Access-Request to the server
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: the access device (switch or AP) is the RADIUS client.

options.text: The access device sends an Access-Request to the RADIUS server
options.rationale: True.

options.text: An Access-Challenge asks for more information, such as an MFA code
options.rationale: True.

options.text: An Access-Reject tells the access device to deny the user
options.rationale: True.

questions.explanation: In the RADIUS login process, the user's credentials go to the access device, which sends an Access-Request to the server. The server answers Accept, Reject, or Challenge, and the access device acts on it.
questions.discriminator_tested: The access device is the RADIUS client, not the user's endpoint.

questions.stem: Which password policy rule does NOT make passwords harder to guess?

options.text: Allowing users to reuse their previous password
options.rationale: Correct choice: reuse weakens the policy.

options.text: A minimum length of 14 characters
options.rationale: Length is the strongest single improvement.

options.text: Blocking common and previously leaked passwords
options.rationale: This removes the easiest guesses.

options.text: Allowing long passphrases that include spaces
options.rationale: This makes long passwords easier to use.

questions.explanation: Password length and complexity make passwords resist guessing, and length adds more strength than complexity alone. Allowing reuse undoes those gains.
questions.discriminator_tested: Length adds more strength than complexity alone.

questions.stem: An account locks for 15 minutes after five failed login attempts. Which attack does this password lockout most directly slow down?

options.text: Online brute force against the login page
options.rationale: Correct: the attacker can make only a few guesses per lockout period.

options.text: Offline cracking of a stolen password hash
options.rationale: Offline guessing never touches the login page, so lockout never triggers.

options.text: Shoulder surfing
options.rationale: The watcher sees the real password; no guessing is involved.

options.text: Phishing for credentials
options.rationale: The user hands over the real password; there are no failed attempts.

questions.explanation: Password lockout locks an account after a set number of failed attempts, which counters online brute force. It does nothing against attacks that obtain the real password or guess offline.
questions.discriminator_tested: Lockout counters online brute force.

questions.stem: Which statement about 802.1X is NOT true?

options.text: It encrypts all traffic on the switch port after the user logs in
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: 802.1X controls access to the port; it doesn't encrypt the traffic.

options.text: It is port-based access control
options.rationale: True.

options.text: The port stays blocked for normal traffic until the device authenticates
options.rationale: True.

options.text: It typically uses a RADIUS server as the authentication server
options.rationale: True.

questions.explanation: 802.1X is port-based access control: the port passes only authentication traffic until the device authenticates. It decides access; it doesn't encrypt the traffic that follows.
questions.discriminator_tested: 802.1X keeps the port blocked until success; it controls access, not encryption.

questions.stem: In an 802.1X deployment, software built into a laptop sends the user's credentials as soon as the laptop is plugged into a switch port. Which 802.1X component is that software?

options.text: Supplicant
options.rationale: Correct: the client side that requests access.

options.text: Authenticator
options.rationale: The authenticator is the switch or WAP that enforces the decision.

options.text: Authentication server
options.rationale: The authentication server is the RADIUS server that makes the decision.

options.text: Captive portal
options.rationale: A captive portal is a web login page, not an 802.1X component.

questions.explanation: The 802.1X components are the supplicant (client), the authenticator (switch or WAP), and the authentication server (RADIUS). The authenticator enforces; the server decides.
questions.discriminator_tested: Supplicant = client; authenticator = switch or WAP; server = RADIUS.

questions.stem: A laptop passes authentication, but its posture check finds missing patches. The NAC policy places it on a remediation network that can reach only the update server. What does this show about the NAC process?

options.text: Its outcomes are policy-driven and need not be all-or-nothing: full, restricted, quarantine, or deny
options.rationale: Correct: the device got restricted access, not a simple yes or no.

options.text: NAC can only allow or deny a device
options.rationale: Quarantine and restricted access are also possible outcomes.

options.text: The quarantine was caused by a failed authentication
options.rationale: Authentication succeeded; the posture check failed.

options.text: The quarantine turned the laptop into a honeypot
options.rationale: A honeypot is a decoy system, unrelated to quarantine.

questions.explanation: In the NAC process, a device connects, is identified and assessed, and policy then sets its access level. The outcome is policy-driven and need not be all-or-nothing.
questions.discriminator_tested: NAC outcomes are policy-driven, not all-or-nothing.

questions.stem: Which two statements correctly separate profiling from posturing? (Choose two.)

options.text: Profiling identifies what a device is, such as its type or class
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Posturing checks a device's health and compliance
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Profiling checks whether the antivirus definitions are current
options.rationale: Checking health is posturing.

options.text: Posturing works out whether a device is a printer or a phone
options.rationale: Working out device type is profiling.

options.text: Both verify the user's password
options.rationale: Checking passwords is authentication.

questions.explanation: Profiling identifies what a device is from observed attributes. Posturing checks its health and compliance. Neither one verifies the user's identity.
questions.discriminator_tested: Profiling = device type; posturing = device health.

questions.stem: One laptop, with valid credentials, is quarantined every time it connects, while a colleague's laptop gets full access. Both users hold the same role. What is the most likely reason?

options.text: The laptop fails its posture assessment, for example because of missing patches or disabled antivirus
options.rationale: Correct: same identity checks and same role, but a different device health result.

options.text: The user is typing the wrong password
options.rationale: The user authenticates successfully.

options.text: The user's role isn't authorized for network access
options.rationale: The colleague with the same role gets full access.

options.text: The laptop is being profiled as a printer
options.rationale: Nothing suggests a profiling error; quarantine points to device health.

questions.explanation: Posturing checks a device's health and compliance, such as patches, antivirus, and configuration. It is separate from identity and role, which is why two users with the same role can get different results.
questions.discriminator_tested: Posture is about device health, not identity or role.

questions.stem: Which statement about BYOD is NOT true?

options.text: Personal devices can be trusted as much as managed company laptops, since employees own them
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: they are unmanaged, so their state is unknown.

options.text: It means personally owned devices accessing organizational resources
options.rationale: True.

options.text: The devices are varied and unmanaged
options.rationale: True.

options.text: It calls for NAC, posture checks, and segmentation
options.rationale: True.

questions.explanation: BYOD means personally owned devices accessing organizational resources. Because they are unmanaged and varied, they need NAC, posture checks, and segmentation.
questions.discriminator_tested: BYOD devices are unmanaged, so they need extra controls.

questions.stem: What separates guest network isolation from BYOD onboarding?

options.text: Guest isolation keeps visitors on a separate, internet-only segment; BYOD onboarding gives employees' own devices controlled access to some organizational resources
options.rationale: Correct: guests get the internet only, while BYOD devices reach some internal resources under controls.

options.text: They are the same thing
options.rationale: They serve different users and grant different access.

options.text: BYOD devices always get internet-only access
options.rationale: The point of BYOD is to reach organizational resources, under controls.

options.text: Guest isolation requires a persistent agent on every visitor's device
options.rationale: Guests are simply segmented; no permanent agent is needed.

questions.explanation: Guest network isolation places visitors on a separate segment with internet-only access. BYOD gives personal devices controlled access to organizational resources through NAC and posture checks.
questions.discriminator_tested: Guest isolation = internet only; BYOD = controlled access to internal resources.

questions.stem: Which statement about a captive portal is NOT true?

options.text: It encrypts the wireless traffic once the user logs in
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: a captive portal is a gate, not encryption.

options.text: It intercepts a new user's first web request
options.rationale: True.

options.text: It requires a login or acceptance of terms before granting access
options.rationale: True.

options.text: It is commonly used for guest and BYOD onboarding
options.rationale: True.

questions.explanation: A captive portal intercepts a new user's first request and requires a login or acceptance before granting access. It gates onboarding; it doesn't encrypt wireless traffic.
questions.discriminator_tested: A captive portal is an onboarding gate, not encryption.
